Self-Healing Test Automation in Regression Testing

benjination2@gmail.com • 10/30/2025


Test automation is an essential part of modern and complex online distributed system software.
Until recently, the method of testing deployed software required the use of static object locators
that can find and interact with specific elements on a webpage. The main issue with this kind of
testing is that any minor UI (User Interface) change like renaming a button or variable will cause
this type of test to fail. The time spent on modifying tests typically outweighs the time spent on
actual implementation.
Now that we have experienced a significant advance in AI technology, there are options for
automated testing that were never available before. Self-Healing Test Automation (SHTA) is an
integration of artificial intelligence into test automation frameworks. This method automatically
detects, analyzes, and repairs failed tests without any human interaction at all. This creates a
major change for the workflow of designers and programmers that specialize in online
distributed system software, as they are allowed to focus more on implementation and less on
redesigning test scripts. Using this method, if a programmer makes a minor UI change, the test
will not automatically fail, but instead the AI will attempt to recognize the issue to determine if it
is a legitimate test failure. If the program is legitimately failing the test, it will report the failed
test back, but if it's something trivial like a name change, the AI corrects the test and reports the
change back to the programmer. SHTA addresses a real market challenge and aims to prevent
potential bottlenecks and enable continuous delivery and innovation.
ACCELQ's Self-Healing Framework:
In my research on this topic, I found an article by Geosley Andrades with ACCELQ (Not an
acronym, but a business specializing in AI-powered codeless test automation) that I found
particularly enlightening. Andrades frames self-healing test automation as an evolutionary
necessity rather than merely a convenient feature (Andrades, 2025). He recognizes as I have that
traditional testing methods do not accommodate emerging technologies, and that minor UI
changes are creating massive difficulties for modern programmers. In the article, Andrades offers
an excellent 5 step process of how SHTA-AI actually works.
1. Detection: The framework identifies that an element is missing or has been modified.
2. Analysis: The algorithm analyzes the UI to identify an alternative matching element.
3. Adaptation: Outdated locator scripts are updated with the new information dynamically.
4. Validation: The modified test is executed to ensure correctness.
5. Learning: The system improves by learning from past fixes.
This framework gained credibility by demonstrating an 80% reduction in required test
maintenance with an unnamed e-commerce website (Andrades, 2025). Moore’s law says that
processing speeds every 18-24 months. For innovation to keep pace with rapidly advancing
technologies, the processes must be streamlined and improved whenever possible. SHTA is
allowing innovation to move faster than ever before by eliminating time wasted on modifying
static tests.
I expanded my knowledge on the subject by exploring other sources that supported Andrades’
system. The other works cited below is an article by Vincent Nguyen called Self-Healing test
Automation: A practical guide, and a work called the World Quality Report for 2024-25 by many
different contributors, but specifically a man named Muji Majzoub. Majzoub is the Chief Product
Officer with Opentext. He conducted a survey of 1,775 Quality Engineering professionals from
33 different countries that confirmed that technologies in software development were no longer
aspirational goals, but operational necessities (Majzoub, 2024). This study also showed that
nearly seventy percent of respondents were using some form of generative Ai, and seventy-five
percent were actively seeking and planning to implement new testing technologies. This
momentum that is apparent in modern programmers confirms Andrades outlook that this
emerging technology is a necessity, and not just a convenience feature.
This dramatic shift in the number of companies using generative AI demonstrates the industries
movement to AI-powered solutions and technical implementation strategies which supports both
Andrades’ claim and the article written by Vincent Nguyen. Nguyen is a QA consultant with
Katalon, a separate software company that also AI-powered automation testing. The thing that set
Nguyen’s article aoart from the other two is that he provides a comprehensive guide that offers
technical validation for Andrades’ Self-Healing framework. Nguyen’s article examines the
method from an implementation viewpoint. Nguyen independently confirms that "test scripts
break" is "one of the most frustrating parts of test automation," directly supporting Andrades'
assertion that traditional locator-based testing creates unsustainable maintenance burdens
(Nguyen, 2025). He suggests the use of redundancy in programs with locator strategies as back-
up for the Ai-powered system. Andrades’ claim that such technologies can exist is fortified by the
fact that the service is already being provided by companies like Katalon. Not only is Self-
Healing testing automation now possible, but it is likely to become a necessary testing method
for all deployed systems as new technologies emerge.
